summary:
Guainía department lies in Colombia's frontier 'orden público' belt, where armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct. That is the operative security context for a trans visitor here. No department-specific legal or enforcement deviation is on record for Guainía, so exposure is assessed against the national framework and its enforcement record.

The framework a trans visitor stands under is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Passports issued within Colombia have offered three gender options (male, female, X) since August 2023, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since the Constitutional Court's 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, and adoption by same-sex couples since November 2015. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. One assessment puts the figure at one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025, 63% above 2024, amid territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ violence nationally. CNN 'As Equals' follow-up reporting of 6 August 2025 documented killings continuing after the Millerey case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025. He praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers distributed on streets and via WhatsApp, naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Nationally, eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023.

Targeted killings of trans people also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
The armed-group "social cleansing" pattern is documented in departments neighbouring the frontier belt rather than in Guainía itself. Caquetá and Guajira supply the concrete evidence: death-threat ultimatums delivered to named trans women, flyer and WhatsApp kill lists, and displacement. Guainía's position in the same frontier belt means the mechanism is plausibly present, but the sources do not itemise incidents inside the department.

Discrimination operates through livelihood as well as violence. Reporting from Caquetá found that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which narrows the practical options for a trans person stranded or working in the region and concentrates exposure to the groups driving the killings.

Detention is a distinct exposure point. A Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system, which indicates both that the problem reached the courts and that a visitor detained here enters a system with a documented history of mistreatment.

Comparatively, the national homicide counts and the departmental picture diverge in evidentiary quality: the national totals are counted by the Attorney General's Office and by NGOs, while Guainía has no comparable local tally in the sources. The frontier belt and the armed groups' conduct regulation are what a visitor actually meets on the ground here, and that is a governance fact rather than a statutory one.
localsOnly:
Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling.

Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X), and from November 2025 national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement.

The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, the first wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016, after three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights. Full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration followed in November 2015.

Residents deprived of liberty have judicial protection: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman in custody, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so the statutory layer beyond the notary procedure and court rulings is not yet settled.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Guainía-specific finding on trans safety, incidents or enforcement is available in the inventory; the department's own reference page yielded nothing usable for this record. Whether armed-group conduct regulation has been documented within Guainía's boundaries, as opposed to the wider frontier belt, remains unresolved on the sources supplied.

The sources give no local homicide or threat counts for Guainía, so the national figures (35 LGBTI murders January to May 2025; one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025; 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025; 41 trans people killed in 2023) cannot be apportioned to this department. The two counts of trans killings in 2025 come from different reporting exercises and are not reconciled here.

How the national document, healthcare and police-protection rules are applied in practice by notaries, hospitals and police in Guainía is not sourced. Availability of trans-specific healthcare, safe accommodation and vetted facilities in the department is likewise not addressed by any source in the inventory.

Whether the Attorney General's Office or the Special Jurisdiction for Peace has opened any case connected to violence against LGBT people in Guainía is unresolved; the prosecutions cited here arise in other parts of the country.
